summary: The note is a Wikipedia-derived excerpt about the United Kingdom's intellectual and political history. It covers the British Empiricism and Scottish Common Sense philosophical traditions, along with utilitarianism as developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. It also traces how the UK's formation and borders changed from the 1707 Treaty of Union through the 1922 partition of Ireland, and notes the remnants of the British Empire.
one_line: Overview of the United Kingdom's philosophical traditions and the historical evolution of its borders and empire.
key_facts: The United Kingdom is famous for the tradition of 'British Empiricism', which holds that only knowledge verified by experience is valid.
'Scottish Philosophy' is sometimes referred to as the 'Scottish School of Common Sense'.
The most famous philosophers of British Empiricism are John Locke, George Berkeley and David Hume.
Dugald Stewart, Thomas Reid and William Hamilton were major exponents of the Scottish 'common sense' school.
Utilitarianism was first used by Jeremy Bentham and later by John Stuart Mill in his short work Utilitarianism.
Wales had been conquered and annexed by the Kingdom of England before the creation of the UK.
The United Kingdom created in 1707 by the Treaty of Union between England and Scotland encompassed all of Great Britain.
The Kingdom of Ireland merged with this state in 1801 to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
Five-sixths of Ireland seceded from the UK in 1922, leaving the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
There are fourteen British Overseas Territories, the remnants of the British Empire.
At its height in the 1920s, the British Empire encompassed almost a quarter of the world's land mass.
The British Empire was the largest empire in history.
British influence can be observed in the language, culture and legal systems of many of its former colonies.
